processing: The flower heads or petals of pot marigold are dried and infused, with no further processing.
harvest_season: Picked while the plant is in flower; it blooms over a long season, and no single picking is prized.
appearance_dry: Loose bright orange and yellow petals, sometimes with whole dried flower heads.
appearance_wet: Soft, slippery orange petals that keep much of their colour.
taste_profile: Mild, earthy and slightly bitter, with a faint peppery edge and honeyed undertone.

brewing.notes: Steep covered for 5 to 7 minutes and strain well. Cold-brewing in the fridge for 12 to 18 hours gives a milder, sweeter cup. A little lemon or honey suits it.

vintage_note: Sold as dried petals or whole flowers without a vintage, usually by herbal shops. As with other dried flowers, buy recent stock: colour is the best quick guide, and dull brown petals have gone stale.
description:
Calendula tea is made from the petals of pot marigold, Calendula officinalis, and is a staple of European herb shelves. Do not confuse it with Tagetes marigolds, which share the English word.

There is no real processing beyond drying. What you are buying is the colour and mild flavour of the petals, so it is the look of the flowers that tells you about quality.

The cup is gentler than the colour suggests: mildly bitter, earthy, a little peppery. It is more a soft herbal background than a big flavour, so it often goes into blends, and lemon or honey helps on its own.

It belongs to the daisy family, so anyone with ragweed or daisy allergies should be careful, and it is generally advised against in pregnancy. Most claims made for it are traditional rather than clinically supported.
history:
Calendula was a common ingredient in herbal remedies in medieval Europe, and Russian references list the tea as antiseptic and astringent. Its Latin name is often linked to the calends, the first day of the month, because the plant blooms almost continuously.

Little is documented about the tea as a distinct drink, including when or where it first became common.
